en-p01.title: The Honeybee's Dance
en-p01.text:
Honeybees live in large colonies, and every member has a job to do. Some bees clean the hive, some guard the entrance, and others fly out to look for flowers. When a worker bee finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a special movement known as the waggle dance. By moving in a figure-of-eight pattern and shaking her body, she tells her sisters where the food is. The angle of the dance shows the direction of the flowers in relation to the sun, and the length of the waggle shows how far away they are.

This remarkable system was studied by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for his work. His findings showed that even small insects can pass on complex information to one another. Today, scientists still study bees to understand how animals communicate.

en-p02.title: Learning to Ride a Bicycle
en-p02.text:
When I was nine, my father bought me a red bicycle on my birthday. I was delighted, but I was also afraid of falling. On the first Sunday, he took me to the empty ground near our house and held the back of the seat while I pedalled. My legs shook, and the handlebar wobbled from side to side.

After an hour I begged him to let me stop, but he only smiled and said, "One more round." Suddenly I noticed that the seat was no longer in his hand. He was standing far behind me, clapping. I had been riding alone for several seconds! The moment I realised it, I lost my balance and fell onto the soft grass. I was not hurt, and I could not stop laughing. That evening I understood that fear often disappears when we keep trying.

en-p03.title: Why Forests Matter
en-p03.text:
Forests cover nearly one-third of the land on Earth, and they are important for all living things. Trees take in carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen, which humans and animals need to breathe. Their roots hold the soil firmly, so heavy rain cannot wash it away easily. Forests are also home to millions of species of plants and animals, many of which are found nowhere else.

Unfortunately, large areas of forest are cut down every year to make room for farms, roads and cities. When forests disappear, the animals lose their homes, and the soil becomes weak. The climate may also change because there are fewer trees to absorb carbon dioxide. To protect the forests, governments must make strict laws, and ordinary citizens should plant more trees and use paper wisely.

en-p04.title: The Vanishing Sparrow
en-p04.text:
Not long ago, the chirping of house sparrows was a familiar morning sound in Indian towns. Today, in many cities, the bird has become a rare sight. Researchers who have studied the problem point to several causes. Modern buildings made of glass and concrete offer few gaps and ledges where sparrows could build nests, unlike the tiled roofs and wooden eaves of older houses. The disappearance of open spaces and small gardens has reduced the insects on which sparrow chicks feed in their first week of life.

Changes in the food habits of people have also played a part. Earlier, grain was cleaned and dried in courtyards, and spilt seeds were an easy meal for sparrows. Now, most families buy packaged food, and little is left on the ground. Some scientists also suspect that radiation from mobile towers may affect the birds, but studies on this point have not reached a firm conclusion.

Conservation groups have begun to respond. They distribute wooden nest boxes, encourage people to keep a bowl of water and grains on their balconies, and celebrate 20 March as World Sparrow Day. Small as these steps may seem, they show that city dwellers can make space for wildlife if they choose to do so.

en-p05.title: The Silk Route
en-p05.text:
The Silk Route was not a single road but a network of trade paths that connected China with Central Asia, India, Persia and Europe. It takes its name from Chinese silk, the most prized good that travelled along it, but merchants carried much more than cloth. Spices, precious stones, tea, paper and metalwork passed from hand to hand, and few traders ever travelled the entire distance. Goods were usually sold from one caravan to the next, and each stage added to the final price.

India occupied an important place in this exchange. Its cotton textiles, pepper and gemstones were in great demand abroad, and the northwestern cities of the subcontinent served as resting points for caravans. Ideas travelled alongside goods. Buddhism, which began in India, spread to Central Asia and China largely because monks accompanied merchants on these routes. Monasteries along the way offered shelter to travellers and, in turn, received donations from rich traders.

The route declined when sea travel became safer and cheaper, and when political upheavals made overland journeys dangerous. Many oasis towns that once flourished on the trade slowly lost their importance. Yet its legacy survives. The routes reminded the world that trade is never only about profit; it also carries languages, religions and arts across distant lands.

en-p06.title: Why Do We Have Leap Years?
en-p06.text:
The Earth takes a little more than 365 days to complete one orbit around the Sun. To be exact, the journey lasts about 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 46 seconds. Our calendar, however, counts only whole days, and so a difference of nearly six hours is left over each year. If nothing were done about it, the calendar would slowly drift away from the seasons. After a hundred years the gap would be about twenty-four days, and the dates of seasonal festivals would shift from one season to another.

To prevent this, an extra day is added to February every fourth year. This gives us a leap year of 366 days. The idea is attributed to Julius Caesar, who introduced it in 45 BCE. Yet adding a day every four years slightly overcorrects, because six hours multiplied by four is a little less than twenty-four hours, though the calendar treats it as a full day. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII therefore introduced a refinement: century years such as 1900 are not leap years unless they are divisible by 400. For this reason 2000 was a leap year while 1900 was not.

The modern calendar is therefore not perfect, but it is remarkably accurate. It takes several thousand years before it drifts a single day out of step with the Sun.

en-p07.title: My Grandmother's Kitchen
en-p07.text:
Everything about my grandmother's kitchen in Lucknow was small except the aromas. It had a single window, a stone slab for grinding spices, and a row of steel boxes whose labels had faded long ago. She never used a recipe book. When I once asked how she knew the quantity of salt, she looked at me with mild surprise and said that her hands remembered it.

As a child I thought this was magic. As an adult, living alone in a rented flat in Pune, I tried to recreate her kheer and failed repeatedly. It was either too sweet or too thin, and it never tasted like hers. I phoned her in frustration. She did not give me measurements. Instead she said, "Stay by the stove and stir slowly. The milk will tell you when it is ready."

I laughed at first, but I followed her advice. Standing patiently, I noticed how the milk thickened and how its smell changed just before it was done. That evening the kheer came out right. I realised that she had not been hiding a secret. She had simply been trusting years of attention, something no written recipe can supply. Whenever I cook now, I try to listen to the stove.

en-p08.title: The Gig Economy
en-p08.text:
In the last decade, a new form of employment has spread across Indian cities. Delivery riders, cab drivers, freelance designers and tutors who find work through mobile applications are often described as part of the "gig economy". Instead of holding a permanent post, a gig worker takes up individual tasks, or "gigs", and is paid for each one. Supporters argue that this arrangement offers freedom that conventional jobs rarely allow. A worker can decide when to log in, which orders to accept and how many hours to put in, and can thereby fit work around studies or family duties. Many young people, especially in smaller towns, have found in such work a first source of independent income.

Yet this flexibility has a price. Because gig workers are classified as independent partners rather than employees, they usually receive no paid leave, no provident fund and no health cover. Their income can fluctuate sharply, depending on demand, weather and the algorithms that assign tasks. Such uncertainty makes it difficult for them to plan loans, rent or savings. A rider who falls ill for a week may lose not only wages but also the favourable rating that brings future orders. Critics add that the apparent freedom is often illusory, since workers who reject too many assignments can be quietly penalised by the platform.

Policymakers have begun to take notice. The Code on Social Security, passed by Parliament in 2020, for the first time recognised gig and platform workers as a category deserving welfare protection, and some states have drafted their own laws. Economists, however, caution that heavy regulation might discourage companies from creating such jobs at all. The challenge, they say, is to find a balance in which workers gain security without the platforms losing the lightness that made the model attractive. How that balance is struck will shape the working lives of millions of young Indians in the coming years.

en-p09.title: In Praise of Boredom
en-p09.text:
Modern children rarely get bored. A phone, a tablet or a television is always within reach, ready to fill every idle minute. Parents and teachers often welcome this, since a distracted child is a quiet child. Psychologists, however, have begun to ask whether we are depriving children of something valuable. Boredom, they argue, is not merely an irritating gap in activity; it is a signal that pushes the mind to look inward and invent its own amusement. Without such moments, the argument runs, a child never learns to depend on his or her own resources and is left waiting for the next outside stimulus.

Consider what happens when a child is left with nothing to do on a rainy afternoon. After the initial complaints, she may begin to build a fort from cushions, draw an imaginary map or invent a game with elaborate rules. These activities are not trivial. They train the child to set goals, to persist without external rewards and to tolerate the discomfort of an empty hour. In one well-known experiment, adults who first carried out a dull task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, later came up with more creative uses for ordinary objects than those who had not.

None of this means that screens are harmful in themselves, nor that children should be left idle for hours. Educational programmes and games can sharpen skills. The concern is with proportion. Used wisely, they are a servant, not a master. A day in which every pause is filled leaves no room for the slow, wandering thought from which new ideas arise. Teachers might therefore consider building short periods of unstructured time into the school day, much as they schedule games or music. Such pauses, far from being wasted, may prove to be among the most productive moments a child ever has.

en-p10.title: The Forgotten Rivers
en-p10.text:
Many Indian cities began on the banks of rivers. Pataliputra, Varanasi, Delhi and Ahmedabad all grew because water, fertile soil and easy transport met at the same place. For centuries the river was the heart of urban life: people bathed in it, drew drinking water from it, held festivals on its banks and sailed goods along it. Today, in a number of these cities, the same river is hardly noticed. It runs behind high walls, carries sewage and is crossed by traffic without a second glance. Old stairways leading down to the water, now unused in many towns, remain as a reminder of that closeness.

How did this neglect come about? Part of the explanation lies in the pace of growth. As populations multiplied, the drains of new settlements were simply connected to the nearest stream, as this was the quickest and cheapest solution. Factories followed the same path, and over time the river was treated less as a neighbour and more as an open drain. Piped water, introduced to supply homes, further loosened the link between citizens and their river, because people no longer needed to visit the bank to fetch water. What was once a shared resource slowly came to be seen as a nuisance, or as vacant land awaiting use.

Recent efforts at revival suggest that the damage is not necessarily permanent. In several cities, treatment plants have been set up to stop untreated sewage from reaching the water, and walkways along the banks have encouraged residents to return. Experts caution, however, that cosmetic beautification must not be mistaken for restoration. A river is a living system with its own flow, and a stretch of clean-looking water behind concrete embankments may still be ecologically dead. Real recovery requires letting the river keep enough water, and enough space, to behave like a river once more. Such patience will cost more than a quick makeover, but the results last longer.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How honey is made inside a hive
Why bees guard the entrance of their hive
The life of the scientist Karl von Frisch
How honeybees tell one another where food can be found
questions.e: Most of the passage explains the waggle dance, through which bees share the location of food.

questions.q: According to the passage, what does the length of the waggle show?
o: How far away the flowers are
How many flowers there are
Where the sun is at that time
How sweet the nectar is
questions.e: The first paragraph says the length of the waggle shows the distance of the flowers. The angle shows direction.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage?
o: Some bees guard the entrance of the hive
Bees turn nectar into honey
The dance follows a figure-of-eight pattern
The angle of the dance is related to the sun
questions.e: The passage never talks about honey-making. The other three points are all stated in the first paragraph.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that the waggle dance is useful to the colony because it
o: makes the queen bee lay more eggs
keeps enemies away from the hive
helps other bees reach a food source without searching blindly
tells the bees when the sun will set
questions.e: The dance gives direction and distance of the food, so other bees can go straight to it.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to REMARKABLE as used in the passage.
o: Ordinary
Doubtful
Quiet
Extraordinary
questions.e: 'Remarkable' means worthy of notice, that is, extraordinary. 'Ordinary' is its opposite.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: My First Ride with My Father's Help
A Dangerous Accident
The History of the Bicycle
A Birthday Party at School
questions.e: The passage describes how the writer learnt to cycle with his father's support, so this title fits best.

questions.q: Where did the writer's father take him to practise?
o: A busy road
An empty ground near their house
The school playground
A neighbour's garden
questions.e: The passage says that father took him 'to the empty ground near our house'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: The bicycle was a birthday present
The father let go of the seat while the writer was riding
The writer injured his knee badly when he fell
The writer fell onto soft grass
questions.e: The writer says he 'was not hurt', so a serious injury is not mentioned. The other statements are in the passage.

questions.q: The father's words 'One more round' suggest that he
o: was angry with the boy
wanted to buy another bicycle
was tired of waiting
felt his son was close to riding on his own
questions.e: He smiled and then quietly let go of the seat, which shows he believed the boy was nearly ready.

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to DELIGHTED as used in the passage.
o: Unhappy
Eager
Proud
Pleased
questions.e: 'Delighted' means very pleased. 'Unhappy' is the opposite.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: How to Grow Vegetables at Home
The Importance of Protecting Forests
Roads and Cities of the Future
The Life of Wild Animals
questions.e: The passage explains why forests are valuable and how they can be saved.

questions.q: According to the passage, what do the roots of trees do?
o: They release oxygen
They attract rain
They hold the soil firmly
They shelter wild animals
questions.e: The passage says roots hold the soil so that heavy rain cannot wash it away.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: Forests are home to many species
Trees take in carbon dioxide
Forests are cleared to build roads
Forests bring heavy rainfall to deserts
questions.e: Nothing is said about rain in deserts. The other three points are in the passage.

questions.q: What can be concluded about the loss of forests?
o: It harms wildlife as well as the soil and climate
It benefits farmers permanently
It has no effect on animals
It affects only the people in cities
questions.e: The passage says animals lose homes, the soil weakens and the climate may change.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to STRICT as used in the passage.
o: Gentle
Stern
Weak
Unclear
questions.e: 'Strict laws' are firm and stern laws. 'Gentle' and 'weak' would be opposite in sense.

questions.q: The passage is mainly about
o: the dangers of mobile towers to all birds
the history of World Sparrow Day
the reasons for the decline of sparrows in cities and the steps taken to help them
the architecture of modern buildings
questions.e: The first two paragraphs give causes of the decline and the last describes conservation efforts.

questions.q: According to the passage, what do sparrow chicks feed on in their first week?
o: Grain dried in courtyards
Packaged food
Seeds placed on balconies
Insects
questions.e: The first paragraph says that insects are what chicks feed on in their first week.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given as a reason for the decline of sparrows?
o: Excessive use of pesticides on farms
Few gaps and ledges for nests in modern buildings
Loss of open spaces and small gardens
Less spilt grain because people buy packaged food
questions.e: Pesticides are not mentioned. The other three causes appear in the first two paragraphs.

questions.q: The writer's attitude towards the conservation efforts is best described as
o: scornful
appreciative and hopeful
alarmed
indifferent
questions.e: The writer calls the steps small yet says they show city dwellers can make room for wildlife, which is a hopeful view.

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to ENCOURAGE as used in the passage.
o: Persuade
Support
Discourage
Invite
questions.e: 'Encourage' means to give support or hope. 'Discourage' is the opposite.

o: The Rise of Chinese Silk Weavers
Indian Spices in the Markets of Europe
Travelling Alone Across Deserts
The Silk Route: A Network of Trade and Ideas
questions.e: The passage covers goods, ideas and the decline of the whole network, not a single product or journey.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did goods cost more by the time they reached their destination?
o: Each stage of resale added to the price
Traders paid a tax at every monastery
Silk was always scarce
Caravans were attacked by robbers
questions.e: The first paragraph states that goods were sold from caravan to caravan and each stage added to the price.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
o: Monks travelling with merchants helped Buddhism reach China
Most merchants travelled the entire length of the route themselves
Monasteries sheltered travellers
Indian cotton and pepper were in demand abroad
questions.e: The passage says that few traders ever travelled the entire distance, so the statement is contrary to it.

questions.q: The last sentence suggests that the writer sees trade as
o: purely a way of earning money
a cause of religious conflict
a means of cultural exchange as well as of profit
something that ended with the Silk Route
questions.e: The writer says trade is 'never only about profit' and that it carries languages, religions and arts.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to UPHEAVALS as used in the passage.
o: Celebrations
Agreements
Surpluses
Disturbances
questions.e: 'Political upheavals' are sudden and violent disturbances, which made journeys dangerous.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Why the Calendar Needs Leap Years
The Life of Julius Caesar
How the Earth Spins on Its Axis
Festivals and the Seasons
questions.e: The passage explains the reason for leap years and how the rules were refined.

questions.q: According to the passage, who introduced the rule about century years?
o: Julius Caesar
Pope Gregory XIII
Augustus
Pope Leo X
questions.e: The passage says that Pope Gregory XIII introduced the refinement in 1582. Julius Caesar introduced the basic leap year.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: Julius Caesar introduced the leap year in 45 BCE
An extra day is added to February in a leap year
The leap year was first introduced in 1582
The year 2000 was a leap year
questions.e: The passage says that the leap year came from Julius Caesar in 45 BCE; 1582 saw only a refinement.

questions.q: According to the rules described in the passage, which of the following years will NOT be a leap year?
questions.e: 2100 is a century year not divisible by 400, so it is not a leap year. 2000 and 2400 are divisible by 400, and 2024 is divisible by 4.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to REFINEMENT as used in the passage.
o: Improvement
Reduction
Delay
Replacement
questions.e: A refinement is a small change that improves something. Gregory's rule improved Caesar's system.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Kheer is the most difficult sweet to prepare
Real cooking skill comes from patient attention and experience rather than from measurements
Grandmothers should write down all their recipes
Living alone makes cooking easier
questions.e: The writer learns that his grandmother's skill rested on years of attention, which no written recipe can give.

questions.q: In which city did the writer live as an adult?
o: Lucknow
Delhi
Pune
Mumbai

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: The kitchen had a stone slab for grinding spices
The writer's first attempts at kheer failed
The grandmother advised the writer to stir slowly
The grandmother sent exact measurements by post
questions.e: The passage says she did not give any measurements. The other points are all stated.

questions.q: When the grandmother said that her hands remembered the quantity of salt, she meant that
o: years of practice had made her judgement almost automatic
she had written the amount on her hands
she was too old to read recipes
she followed a secret recipe card

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to MILD as used in the passage.
o: Gentle
Intense
Slight
Polite
questions.e: 'Mild surprise' is slight surprise; 'intense' is the opposite. Gentle and slight are close to 'mild'.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
o: The gig economy has solved the problem of unemployment in India
Platforms should be banned from hiring independent workers
The gig economy offers flexibility but little security, and policymakers are trying to balance the two
Gig workers earn more than permanent employees
questions.e: The passage describes the freedom and the insecurity of gig work and then the search for a regulatory balance.

questions.q: According to critics, why is the freedom of gig workers often 'illusory'?
o: Workers must log in at fixed hours
Platforms pay them a fixed monthly salary
They cannot choose their own tasks at all
Workers who refuse many assignments may be quietly penalised

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?

Gig workers usually get no paid leave
Their income varies with demand and weather
The Code on Social Security recognised platform workers

questions.q: The economists' caution suggests that
o: gig work should be abolished
very strict rules could reduce the number of gig jobs on offer
platforms already provide enough security
state laws are better than central laws
questions.e: They warn that heavy regulation 'might discourage companies from creating such jobs at all'.

Temporary
Deceptive
Generous
questions.e: 'Illusory' means based on an illusion, that is, not real or deceptive. 'Genuine' is the opposite.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
o: Screens are the main cause of poor school results
Children should never be left alone
Teachers should replace games with quiet hours
Unstructured, even boring, time can stimulate creativity and should be allowed to children
questions.e: The writer argues that boredom pushes the mind to invent, and recommends short unstructured periods for children.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest teachers might do?
o: Include short periods of unstructured time in the school day
Ban mobile phones in classrooms
Give more homework
Replace music lessons with games
questions.e: The last paragraph proposes building short unstructured periods into the school day, as games or music are scheduled.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: Parents often welcome a child being distracted
Screen use damages the eyesight of young children
Educational games can sharpen skills
Boredom can push the mind to invent its own amusement
questions.e: Eyesight is never mentioned. In fact the writer says that screens are not harmful in themselves.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the writer's position on screens?
o: Screens are useless for education
Screens should be allowed for unlimited hours
Screens are not harmful in themselves but should not fill every free moment
Screens should be used only by adults
questions.e: The writer says that screens are not harmful in themselves, and that the real concern is with proportion.

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TRIVIAL as used in the passage.
o: Petty
Minor
Slight
Significant
questions.e: 'Trivial' means of little importance. 'Significant' means important, which is the opposite.

The History of Indian Trade
How to Build Concrete Embankments
Festivals on the Banks of the Ganga

The river had dried up completely

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: Sewage drains were connected to the nearest stream
Factories also disposed of waste in rivers
The government has banned all construction near rivers
Walkways have encouraged residents to return to the banks

o: concrete embankments always harm cities

rivers can never be revived
the appearance of clean water is not a reliable sign of a healthy river

Costly
Natural
